english_verification.review_scope: Translated all source Markdown before the National Ideas appendix and all 36 non-national-ideas input pointers. Read representative current-Mod history, formation-event, empowerment, and endgame passages; also read two related English Wiki chunks. The Wiki sources are related background only, not a dedicated S30/S90 country history or authority on current mechanics. The primary compared native idea names/descriptions with current English localisation keys (formatting codes stripped); B32 upgraded Farranean originals also use their separate flavour file. Wide source bounds are locator envelopes, not exhaustive line-by-line audits. No formal validators, tests, builds or browser checks were run.
unresolved: The bounded English offline-Wiki search found no dedicated substantive country history for Death Bringing Cobra or Umbral Covenant. The Shadow Covenant article describes a different organization; no identity equivalence is inferred.

The Yezel Mora Coven article supports only related background about Ilfanill’s cultivation of the Death Bringing Cobra leader and her child; it does not establish that the Shadow Covenant and Umbral Covenant are identical.
The ordinary non-betrayal ending trigger is statically disabled; whether another runtime event bypasses it remains unverified in-game.

Not every empowerment value, random ritual, dynamic mission path, or endgame event was audited. Community accounts cited in the source article are development-branch experiences, not confirmation of current stable mechanics.

The Chinese summary/assessment says kin-and-unborn-child sacrifice. Current English flavor_dbc.1.d/2.d attributes kin deaths to enemies and offers the living unborn child to Ilfanill; the Wiki also identifies that child as the later Vile One. The English article flags this source discrepancy. Chinese conclusions and the existing value score remain frozen pending a separately authorised research correction.

rationale.campaign_length: S30 has 10 direct missions; after formation, S90 has 87 direct missions and dynamic regional branches.
rationale.colonization: The main expansion loop relies on conquest and rifts, not traditional colonization.
rationale.complexity: Five empowerment categories, essence capacity, dynamic regional missions, cultural assimilation, and project gates must be planned in parallel.
rationale.dark_story: Sacrificing kin and an unborn child, harvesting suffering, massacres, looting, forced assimilation, and planar sacrifice all belong to the main story. Source caveat: the current English opening attributes the kin’s deaths to enemies and describes offering the unborn child, not proof that Kuende killed those relatives or that child.
rationale.difficulty: The country is extremely powerful, but manpower, corruption, mission gates, and endgame resource demands make mistakes costly.
rationale.diplomacy: The alliance with the Coven of Yezel Mora is crucial; most other diplomacy serves conquest and cultural integration.
rationale.early_pressure: S30 has a small territory amid competing warlords, so the manpower and corruption costs of its special army quickly become apparent.
rationale.magic_artifice_intensity: Shadow Empowerments, special troops, rifts, three magical projects, and planar convergence make up the entire gameplay package.
rationale.narrative_density: The purge war, bargain with the hags, formation pivot, and sacrificial or betrayal ending form a continuous narrative.
rationale.tall_play: Development, production, and mage-tower gates exist, but mainly serve expansion and magical projects.
rationale.trade_economy: Production buildings and high-development provinces matter, but trade is not central to the country’s fantasy.
rationale.warfare: The warlord prologue, dynamic regional conquest, looting, and enormous casualty gates keep war central throughout.

identity.appearance: A 1444 starting country; completing its dedicated ten-mission prologue triggers an event that forms S90 Umbral Covenant. Other eligible Shadow Pact countries in Sarhal can also form S90 by general decision.

survey_region.note: Death Bringing Cobra S30 itself corresponds to Rank 23 Death Bringing Cobra. The local article records its successor S90 Umbral Covenant separately at Rank 12 (Region: Sarhal). The successor’s region is not substituted for its predecessor; the production identity remains S30.

national_ideas.scope_note: National traditions, seven national ideas and ambition only; optional idea groups and racial/government bonuses are excluded. Conditional alternatives are separate, not stacked. Accepting new ideas on formation depends on the actual event/decision and player choice.

description.text:
Many centuries ago, Bamaliwuni was a place scattered with many squabbling tribes, very unlike the warlords that developed later. They lived under the yoke of the Djinnakah Sultanate that established tribute over each of them, controlling the entire region from their outposts at the mouths of large rivers. When this empire collapsed, a power vacuum emerged, throwing the tribes into endless war that ended in a formation of a state that people call Bwa Dakinshi, the same one that the warlords struggle endlessly to recreate. But the part of that history that the warlords do not remember is that this state still lives.

The clan and the heirs of the great unifier Mauya Venomrisker are still standing, hidden in the mountains, despite the many rebellions that faced them; as long as they stand, no one can dare name themselves Bwa Dakinshi.

description.text:
Not so long ago, the clan of Death Bringing Cobra was on the verge of regaining their lost heritage. The entire north of Bamaliwuni stood open to them after their capture of Inshibonde and no one could stand against them; the sprawling state of Katidariga had just collapsed, the warlords of Gumti had already succumbed and offered their services, while Kaziradoka stayed encircled with no allies to support them.

But no one suspected the enemy to come from within. The traitor named Kwizera struck in a swift coup that murdered most of our clan. The remnants escaped to the high mountains, led by Kuende, the first wife of the matriarch. Yet in her guidance, a dark truth was hidden, as she sold herself to the Hags a long time ago. No one is truly aware of the scale of the danger she truly poses, but one thing is known. The child she took with herself, the true heir to the Bwa Dakinshi, bears the same dark aura as her, and only time will tell what dark thoughts possess Her mind.

description.text:
The reality of a warlord society is ruthless. Competitors are plenty and the resources scarce and centered in few places. Those who are not strong enough find themselves working for the sole benefit of their local warlords, while those who dare try to fight the existing hierarchy, duel their way into the higher position amongst the Munitaragomo to hopefully reach the top of the hierarchy as the Vitaragomo of the warband.
While this means that only competent fighters advance to the top, this also adds to the instability of the region, as warlords incessantly rebel against their former overlords.

description.text:
It isn’t really a secret that warlords largely despise each other. The net of personal grudges between the Vitaragomo has been dense for years with few ends unconnected, effectively stymying any attempt at diplomacy that is not a simple demand for capitulation.
So far goes this devotion to not liking each other that some animosities are now built artificially, by a peculiar custom that emerged something over hundred years ago.

The lesser warlords sit down with the Vitaragomo near a large table. Some of them see paper for the first time in their lives, as they hear the name of the warlord that is the topic of the meeting. For the following six hours, the meeting will proceed as its members write out a series of convoluted and obscene insults towards a certain warlord; this is then sent to the victim, who upon delivery must read it aloud to the laughter of his subjects, risking great shame if he doesn’t.

description.text:
The demand for iron for weapons and luxuries for the rich never runs out.
Despite the poor state of the economy and the dangers that the region’s trade routes bear, there are still traders brave and insane enough to traverse the lands of Bamaliwuni, looking to secure its riches and carry them to the port cities. The upside is worth it though, as those who manage to make the trip find themselves richer than most Dakinshi, able to afford a lavish lifestyle for the rest of their lives just with a few ventures.

description.text:
Previously serving as the spiritual leaders of the Dakinshi society, the druids of the Beast Memory serve as the reminders of once broken link between humans and animals. Brought up from those magically gifted across the land, they organize themselves at the natural meeting points of animal herds, protecting these vital positions against any interference that would disrupt the natural order.

While typically peaceful in their behavior, the times of strife have proven dangerous enough to change some of the druids' stance to a more offensive one, joining the many warlords of the land in a proactive effort to keep out everyone who does not care about the environment.

description.text: Across the land, there is a common impetus driving every warlord’s mind. A desire to win, to squash one’s opponents under their feet, best them in battle, lay upon their corpses and dance on their graves. The dream of an empire that toppled not so long ago as to be forgotten, but long enough to be romanticised through second-hand nostalgia. The ambition to become something bigger, to be remembered, to be unlike the others. To make oneself known, feared, respected and acknowledged as the single, true unifier to the empire they forged with blood, sweat and tears. This will be the ultimate price of the new Bwa Dakinshi.

description.text:
She was taken as a child by the Night Hag’s Coven. She was not the only one. If one of the Coven detected a baby had been born with incredible latent powers, they would do whatever it took to steal her away and raise her themselves: strike a deal with the parents in exchange for food or power, lure the child away when she was alone, every ace in their collective sleeves shamelessly played. It is estimated that hundreds were whisked away by the Night Hags over the centuries they have plagued Halann, children of every nation and every race.

Such a child was then raised by the hags to be used as a pawn in their nefarious plans for Sarhal. If the child failed to reach expectations, or developed a sudden conscience, they were discarded. The hags’ ideal pawn may have taken hundreds of years to mold, but once complete, would be a weapon they could send forth to carry out their dark bidding independently. The Vile One, as this child would be dubbed, would have the power to unite all peoples beneath her inescapable will.

Human, lizardfolk, gnoll: all would be drawn to her power and unite under her.

description.text:
Shadow Pact is not an inherently evil faith. There is solace to be found in the acceptance of death and the powerlessness you have over your fate. Those who speak of Shadow Pact’s virtue expound upon the peace and clarity you feel in life when you know those of the shadow plane will look after you in death. Yet there is a second face to Shadow Pact. One in which its followers seek not just solace in death, but power over life. Accepting the power of those of the shadow plane, these practitioners call such power into our own.

The Vile One is perhaps the greatest symbol of this face of Shadow Pact. One who was created by the most powerful creatures of the Shadow Plane. Her sole purpose is to grant a nation the power to seize control over all that they wish to call theirs.

description.text:
A nation ruled over by The Vile One changes. A fog spreads like a suffocating blanket over its lands. This fog spreads slowly, blotting out the sun for weeks on end, and obscuring vision such that even leaving your home can be dangerous. Neighbouring countries are not safe from its impact, as the fog neither knows nor cares for borders.

The Vile One’s armies marched under the protection of this fog. This became such a well-known strategy of their armies that people began to panic and flee if the fog spread into their towns, for they knew that meant her armies would soon follow.

description.text: While Sarhal had seen many great conquerors, The Vile One was different. There was no attempt to seek allies, no diplomatic formalities, not even any recognition that other towns or nations had existing hierarchies or rulers through which negotiations could be channelled. Her armies simply marched across borders, struck down any who resisted, and established control over their newly conquered lands. Any dissent was crushed and all previous order was upended. Only those who pledged their allegiance to The Vile One were placed in any position of power. There was no shortage of those who would, even in those areas newly conquered. For they knew, ever since the fog arrived, that this day was coming. There was no stopping the spread of shadow.

description.text: In the core homelands where The Vile One first made herself known, operations were curiously calm and orderly. If you received the call to join the army, it was an honor. If you were placed in administrative positions, that was your duty. If you were a simple laborer or farmer, that too was your role and it was as important as any. Acceptance was absolute. Those who did not agree, or attempted to undermine the cause in any way, disappeared into the fog. Everyone thought everyone else supported the cause, so they did too.

description.text:
When The Vile One fell and the fog was lifted, enemy soldiers attempted to find ringleaders of operations. They captured mayors and chieftains of towns, spoke to villagers and soldiers, and tried to interrogate everyone in the nation to ask why they had sided with a being so obviously evil and destructive. They brought accounts of the horrors her armies had committed, and evidence of what the true final goal of the Night Hags was.

Yet their words did not seem to have any effect. The locals were far too preoccupied with the horrific state of their lands, the decay that they had seemingly only just noticed. The rot was not merely a result of invasion, either. Barren fields, crumbling housing, and decrepit local facilities had just become an accepted norm. Only after her death did the riots start.

description.text: Scholars of Sarhaly history have often debated over the true goals of The Vile One. A growing body of evidence suggests that the simple explanation - that she was simply doing the bidding of the Night Hags - was not a satisfactory answer. It was the actions of The Vile One that caused all of Sarhal to erupt into war, not the infamous ritual the Night Hags had started, for that ritual only started several years after the war began. Military historians have also noted the complete lack of coordination between Yezel Mora and The Vile One. Yes, they fought the same enemies, but not once did they ever fight together. Nobody ever asked her what she was trying to achieve. It would not have crossed anyone’s minds to do so.

It was the eminent Adzalani researcher Tzaaska Cursebreaker who first compellingly identified Kuende as a possible mother for the Vile One. Beyond the broadly correct ethnicity and the emergence of her realm from Dakinshi, Kuende was a known mage who emerged as leader of the moribund Death Bringing Cobra clan before the eventual co-opting of said clan by the Vile One’s Umbral Covenant.

While historians were initially wont to view this shift from clan to Covenant as a subversion or coup, Tzasska argued that Kuende had deliberately prepared her realm for her estranged daughter. As Vitaragomo, Kuende seems to have hoarded raid-wealth, ritual resources and materiél for a purpose she would not explain, directly against the wishes of her own advisors and clanmates. Kuende’s reign of terror was significant in her own right, and the scorched earth tactics pursued by the Vile One, while different in the particulars, seem to echo Kuende’s own.

The rot was not merely a result of invasion, either. Barren fields, crumbling housing, and decrepit local facilities had just become an accepted norm. Only after her death did the riots start.
description.text_en:
When The Vile One fell and the fog was lifted, enemy soldiers attempted to find ringleaders of operations. They captured mayors and chieftains of towns, spoke to villagers and soldiers, and tried to interrogate everyone in the nation to ask why they had sided with a being so obviously evil and destructive. They brought accounts of the horrors her armies had committed, and evidence of what the true final goal of the Night Hags was.

Yet their words did not seem to have any effect. The locals were far too preoccupied with the horrific state of their lands, the decay that they had seemingly only just noticed. The rot was not merely a result of invasion, either. Barren fields, crumbling housing, and decrepit local facilities had just become an accepted norm. Only after her death did the riots start.

description.text:
We know nothing of the Vile One’s intentions; her apparently vast memory and her penchant for telepathic matrices with her closest followers means that her coterie wrote very little down, and in the final days her most devoted adherents made great effort to destroy as many of her records as possible. Kuende, on the other hand, leaves a limited but compelling record. Traumatised by the near-annihilation and humiliation of her clan, Kuende appears to have turned against the very concept of honour itself.

Did the daughter know something of the mother’s will, her utter and complete nihilism? There is no evidence that Kuende ever presented a baby at court, though she alluded obliquely at times to an heir, and was unconcerned with matters of succession. Tzasska Cursebreaker argued in her ‘Addenda’ that the two women likely never met: whatever hatred Kuende felt for Halann, she entrusted to the hags to inculcate in her daughter.

player_overview.avoid_if: Avoid if you dislike sacrifice and suffering narratives, continuous looting and conquest, heavy manpower use, complex mission gates, or an ending built around failure.
player_overview.how_it_plays: Use special troops and omens to end the warlord prologue, then expand through regional conquest to gain Shadow Essence, configure empowerments, pursue assimilation and magical projects, and finally resolve the planar-convergence sacrifice endgame.
player_overview.overview: Begin as a mountain warlord who accepts a hag’s gifts, then use shadow warriors, omens, and a war economy to form Umbral Covenant quickly. The campaign then expands dramatically: conquest creates rifts, Shadow Essence powers a customizable set of empowerments, and major magical projects advance planar convergence. The country is extraordinarily strong, but manpower, corruption, looting, and the final sacrifice keep raising the cost.
player_overview.recommended_for: For players who enjoy extreme-villain stories, very long campaigns, wide conquest, magical resource loadouts, dynamic missions, and dense narrative.
signature_features: A ten-mission warlord prologue ends in a dedicated event that forms Umbral Covenant and shifts to a theocratic magocracy ruled by an immortal mage.
The government interface uses Shadow Essence capacity to support a configurable national loadout drawn from five categories of Shadow Empowerments.
Dynamic regional conquest creates shadow rifts and unlocks magical projects, eventually branching into submission to sacrifice or betrayal in an attempt to survive.
player_overview.tagline: Turn a warlord’s revenge bargain into a shadow empire that consumes Sarhal, tears open the planes, and may ultimately sacrifice itself.

reasons: The formation pivot from S30 to S90 is clear and narratively continuous.
Shadow Essence and five categories of Shadow Empowerments create an unusual national loadout loop.
Dynamic regional missions, rifts, and magical projects directly bind conquest to the mechanics.
10 prologue missions plus 87 post-formation missions support an exceptionally long campaign.
warnings: Special troops and continuous wars rapidly consume manpower and accumulate corruption.
Numerous development, production, cultural-assimilation, looting, and casualty gates can stall the tree.
The text about sacrifice, suffering, and slaughter is extremely dark.
Runtime progression to the non-betrayal ending has not been verified in-game.

values.rationale: Sacrificing kin and unborn children, deliberately causing suffering, looting, forced assimilation, and planar sacrifice are institutional parts of the main campaign; betraying the patron late does not undo earlier actions. Source caveat: the current English opening attributes the kin’s deaths to enemies and describes offering the unborn child, not proof that Kuende killed those relatives or that child.
